blocks.title: Chart variants
blocks.lead: 28 chart types, one primitive (`chart`). Reach for a type by intent — the families below cluster types that solve the same shape of problem. Each card has a tiny live preview; click through to the variant for its full payload and a live render.

blocks.title: Library underneath
blocks.content: All modes are kit-native — no third-party chart library. Cartesian + donut modes render as inline SVG drawn by the oku-chart Custom Element. The bar family renders as plain HTML + CSS, no JavaScript after first paint.

Twenty-eight chart variants grouped by intent. Each card shows a tiny live render so you can compare visual shape at a glance; pick the family that fits what you're communicating, then click through to the variant for the full payload.

cards.title: Categorical
cards.content: One value per category. Sort by value for ranking, by name for lookup.

cards.title: Distribution
cards.content: Shape of one variable. Use when the spread / skew is the story, not a single number.

cards.title: Time series
cards.content: X is time (or any ordered axis). Line when each x has one y; area when stacking matters.

cards.title: Hierarchy / share
cards.content: Parts of a whole. Donut for ≤6 slices; treemap when nesting or many cells beat slices.

cards.title: Relationship
cards.content: Two or more variables interacting. Scatter for raw points; heatmap when density beats individual points.

cards.title: Goal / comparison
cards.content: Actual vs target — the visual answers 'are we there yet?'

cards.title: Conversion
cards.content: Stage-to-stage drop-off through an ordered pipeline.

cards.title: Flow
cards.content: Where the flow goes — links between nodes carry magnitude.

cards.title: Graph
cards.content: Connections between entities. Node degree drives circle radius.

cards.title: Multivariate
cards.content: Many variables at once — when the story lives in correlations, not totals.

cards.title: Circular relationship
cards.content: Pairwise flow / affinity between a small group of entities.

cards.title: Geographic
cards.content: Country / region comparison without map-tile data.

blocks.title: Cartesian — x/y points with axes
blocks.lead: Use when the x-axis is a continuous quantity (or ordered sequence) and you want to show position, slope, or relationships between two numeric dimensions.

blocks.content: One or more series of {x, y} points. Per-point label optional (shown on hover). Per-series colour drawn from the accent / warn / danger / success / muted vocabulary. Axes auto-scale; pass x-scale=log / y-scale=log on the element for log axes.

Same series-of-points contract as scatter — but the renderer connects consecutive points with a polyline. Use when the x-axis is ordered (time, build-number, sequence) and the reader should see slope, not just position. Two or more series stack on the same axes; legend chips at the top-right toggle visibility.
Same shape as line — series of {x, y} points — but the curve is filled down to the baseline. Useful for cumulative metrics over time where magnitude matters as much as direction.

content: Scatter plot with a third dimension encoded as dot size. Each point gains an optional
field; the renderer takes its square root so the dot's AREA is proportional to size (eye reads area, not radius). Useful for cost vs. impact vs. confidence-style decision matrices.

blocks.title: Categorical — value per category
blocks.lead: One bar per item, optionally split into stacks or sub-groups. Use when each row has a single label and value; reach for stacked/grouped when each row has multiple comparable values.

blocks.content: Same payload as stacked-bar, but each series renders as its own thin sub-bar within the row rather than stacking. Use for direct comparison across series within the same category.

blocks.title: Part-to-whole
blocks.lead: A whole divided into named slices. Donut + pie are the classic choices; waffle reads better when the absolute count matters; treemap when the parts have a hierarchy.

content: Single-ring distribution chart. Each
is a
; the renderer normalises values to percentages of the total, draws an arc per slice, and shows the total + a legend on the side.

blocks.content: Same `slices` payload as donut; the only difference is the absence of the centre hole and the centre-readout. Reach for pie when the part-to-whole relationship is the whole story and the absolute total doesn't need an extra glance. Pie reads better than donut for 2–4 slice distributions; for 5+ slices, prefer donut (clearer per-slice legend strip) or stacked-bar.

Dot-matrix breakdown. Default 10×10 grid (= 100 cells). `segments` is a list of `{label, count, color}`; the renderer fills cells in order, one per unit count. The legend lives to the right of the grid with the percentage of each segment.

Area-proportional nested rectangles via squarified layout. `tree[]` is a flat list of `{label, value, color?}` leaves; the largest values occupy the largest rectangles. Labels render only when the rectangle is large enough to fit them legibly. Use for composition (LoC by language, spend by category, traffic by route).

blocks.title: Distribution shape
blocks.lead: How a value's frequency is spread, not its total. Histogram for binned counts; box-plot for quartile summary; ridgeline to compare multiple distributions vertically.

blocks.content: Frequency by bin. Author supplies the binning (`bins[]` with `{lo, hi, count}`). Contiguous bins read as a connected distribution; gaps are allowed but render with the visible gap. Use for distribution shape, latency tail, time-to-event.
Quartiles + whiskers + optional outliers — one row per `boxes[]` entry. Required: `min`, `q1`, `median`, `q3`, `max`. Optional: `outliers: [Number]` rendered as dots beyond the whiskers.

Stacked small-distributions, one per row. `distributions[].values` is a flat sample; the renderer bins each sample into ~30 buckets over the global range. Read for shape comparison across groups (per-region latency, per-cohort engagement).

blocks.title: Trend over time
blocks.lead: Sequence on the x-axis, value on the y. Sparkline for in-line micro-trends; slope for before/after pairs; calendar-heatmap for day-of-year × day-of-week activity.

blocks.content: Inline mini line / area / bar. No axes, no chrome — sized for the line height of surrounding prose. `values` is a flat numeric series. `variant` picks line (default), area (filled), or bar (per-value mini-bars). `end_label` renders to the right of the curve as a small caption (`62%`, `↗`, etc.).

Two-time-point change — left column is `from`, right column is `to`, one slope line per `items[]` entry. The renderer auto-colours rising as success and falling as danger unless an explicit `color` is set. Use this when ‘who went up, who went down’ is the question.

Year-in-cells activity grid. `date_values` is a map of ISO date → numeric value; days missing from the map render faintly to show the calendar shape. Mon, Wed, Fri labels along the left; month names along the top at the first cell of each month.

blocks.title: Flow / conversion
blocks.lead: How a quantity moves between stages or sources. Funnel for ordered drop-off; sankey for arbitrary weighted flows between any pair of nodes.

blocks.content: Conversion-stage drop-off. `stages[]` is an ordered list of `{label, value, color?}`. The renderer draws a tapered band between adjacent stages; the right-hand readout shows the value + percentage of the first stage.

Flow between stages with curved ribbons sized by link value. nodes[] is {id, label?, color?}; links[] is {source, target, value} referencing node ids. The renderer derives the left-to-right column placement from the link graph (BFS depth), stacks nodes within each column by their incoming-or-outgoing total, and routes a cubic-Bezier ribbon between every pair.

blocks.title: Network / relationship
blocks.lead: Edges between nodes. Network for free-form graphs (force-relaxed layout); chord for fully-connected directional flow matrices.

blocks.content: Node-link diagram with a small Fruchterman-Reingold-ish force relaxation (~60 iterations on each render). Best for graphs up to ~50 nodes — bigger structures need a real graph-viz library. nodes[] + links[] share the same shape as sankey. Node radius scales with degree; hovering a node surfaces its label + degree in the tooltip.

Circular relationship diagram. groups[] defines the perimeter sequence (clockwise from 12 o'clock); matrix is an N×N flow matrix where matrix[i][j] is the flow from groups[i] to groups[j]. Each group occupies an outer arc sized by its total in+out flow; ribbons through the centre carry the pairwise flows.

blocks.title: Multivariate / matrix
blocks.lead: More than two dimensions per record. Heatmap for a 2-D grid coloured by value; scatter-matrix for pair-wise scatters across N variables; parallel-coordinates for per-record polylines crossing N axes.

blocks.content: N×M cell grid coloured by value. `cells` is a 2D array (outer = rows, inner = columns). Optional `row_labels` / `col_labels` annotate the edges. `scale` picks the palette family: sequential (one-sided ramp on accent) or diverging (accent for positives, danger for negatives). Hover any cell for the raw value.

N×N grid of mini scatter plots for multivariate correlation reading. variables[] defines each axis; records[] is a flat list of objects keyed by variable id. Domains auto-derive from the records unless declared explicitly.

blocks.title: How to read it
blocks.content: Diagonal cells (top-left to bottom-right) label each variable. Off-diagonal cells plot the column-variable on X against the row-variable on Y. Each cell carries an r= chip in its top-left — Pearson correlation between the two variables (-1 to +1). Values where |r| ≥ 0.7 show in accent-strong: those are the strong relationships worth investigating. Hover any off-diagonal cell to see the pair, n, and r in a tooltip; click to pin.

One vertical axis per variable; each record draws a polyline crossing all axes at its scaled position. Best for spotting multi-variable clusters (lines that bunch together) or outliers (lines that diverge). Optional _label and _color on each record tag it visually.

blocks.title: Goal / progress
blocks.lead: Where a value sits inside a known range (often with a target). Gauge for a single arc; bullet for actual-vs-target with zone bands; radar for multi-axis profile comparison.

blocks.content: Semicircular arc, 0 → max, with a needle / fill at the current value and an optional target tick. Use for single-metric status (SLO budget, runway, uptime) where the gap to target is the point. Optional `zones` paint coloured threshold bands behind the value.

Actual-vs-target on a banded horizontal track — Stephen Few's bullet chart. One row per `tracks[]` entry: `label`, `value` (current), `target` (optional vertical tick), `max` (right-edge), optional `zones` painted behind the value.

N spokes radiating from centre, one filled polygon per series. Best for 3–8 axes and 1–4 series. `axes[].label` names the spoke; optional `axes[].max` overrides per-axis scaling. `series[].values` array must align with `axes` by index.

blocks.title: Geographic
blocks.lead: Value per region laid out on a rough world grid. Use for at-a-glance regional breakdowns without the visual budget of a real choropleth.

blocks.content: Tile cartogram. regions[] is a list of {id, value, label?} where id is an ISO 3166-1 Alpha-2 country code (US, GB, DE, BR, ...) or the synthetic OTH bucket. The kit ships a fixed tile grid (~60 cells) that approximates a flat world map; absent regions render as faint placeholder outlines so the geography stays visible. Cell fill scales with value in a single-hue sequential ramp.
